The main advantages of pelletizing are the creation of consistent physical and chemical characteristics, including an improvement of the feedstock’s homogeneity, quality, flowability, bulk, and energy density. As of December 2024, there were 94 wood pellet plants in the United States with a total annual capacity of 13.4 million tons employing 2,438 people. A number of different feedstocks are used to produce pellets. In 2024, 15.7 million tons of feedstock were used (Figure 35) to produce approximately 10.5 million tons of wood pellets. Woody feedstock prices ranged between $24 and $39 per ton, and feedstock types used to produce wood pellets include other residuals (41%), roundwood/pulpwood (24%), sawmill residuals (16%), and wood product manufacturing residuals (19%) (Figure 35). Production is concentrated in the South (~85%) due to the availability of feedstocks and proximity for export to European Union nations (EIA 2025i). In 2024, 10.7 million tons of wood pellets were produced and 8.9 million (83%) were exported (Figure 36 (EIA 2025i).18 The key market driver for exports is bioenergy policies across northwestern Europe. In 2024, the top exports markets were the United Kingdom (70%), Japan (10%), and the Netherlands (7%) (Krueger 2025). A nationally accepted system for certifying and tracking production volumes (similar to RINs for biofuels) and competitive market pricing for many biochemicals do not yet exist.
